newsitem.title: ITALY: Employers reject Italian govt proposals on pay row.
newsitem.headline: Employers reject Italian govt proposals on pay row.

text.p: Employers on Monday rejected proposals put forward by the Italian government aimed at ending a long-running pay dispute in the crucial metalworkers' and engineering sectors.

"The figures put forward by you cannot provide the basis for a possible conclusion to the negotiations," Federmeccanica, the association of metalworker employers, said in a letter to Labour Minister Tiziano Treu.

Talks between unions and management broke down last week. In a bid to break the impasse, Treu suggested on Sunday that employers should offer workers a pay rise of 200,000 lire ($130) a month for the 1996-1998 contract period.
The move was welcomed by trade unions, who had been asking for 230,000 lire for their 1.7 million members.
Federmeccanica, which had offered a rise of 139,000 lire, said Treu's proposals would help fuel inflation.
"Average salaries would rise by 10.3 percent compared to an inflation rate which according to government targets, will be less than 4.5 percent," the Federmeccanica letter said.
However the federation, which met earlier on Monday, said it still wanted to seek a negotiated solution.
"We are willing to carry on the talks to reach an economic solution in line with beating inflation," it said.

Contracts in the metalworkers' sector, which accounts for some 40 percent of total manufacturing output in Italy, expired in June, and differences between management and unions have widened rather than narrowed in the subsequent negotiations.
At the heart of the quarrel lies a landmark 1993 wage accord which scrapped automatic index-linked salary increases.
Unions say the accord allows for full reimbursement for higher-than-expected inflation in the past contract period. Management disagree.
The metalworkers' pay deal will set the standard for wage rounds under discussion several other industrial sectors.
Many groups, including the Bank of Italy and International Monetary Fund (IMF), have urged constraint on the unions in the fear that a high settlement might set off inflation.
